stpaulwalls-far.name: Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls

guideSights.name: St. Peter's Basilica
guideSights.note: The centre of the Catholic world, this magnificent basilica with its Michelangelo-designed dome has an awe-inspiring interior. This place is huge, but everything is in such proportion that the scale escapes you. However, contrary to popular

guideSights.name: St. Peter's Square
guideSights.note: Most of the ''Piazza di San Pietro'' is actually an oval. There is a small, almost rectangular section immediately in front of the St Peter's and an opening to the Via della Conciliazione opposite the basilica.

guideSights.name: The Vatican Museum
guideSights.note: One of the greatest art galleries in the world, the museum is most famous for its spiral staircase, the Raphael Rooms and the exquisitely decorated Sistine Chapel famous for Michelangelo's frescoes.

guideSights.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
guideSights.note: Perhaps the most fascinating building in Rome. The core of the structure began life as the mausoleum of Emperor Hadrian, built between 135 and 139 AD. Subsequent strongholds built on top of the mausoleum were in turn incorporated into a res

guideSights.name: Passetto di Borgo
guideSights.note: Pope Nicholas III connected Castel Sant'Angelo to St. Peter's by a covered fortified corridor called the Passetto di Borgo. This proved useful for Pope Clement VII during the Sack of Rome (1527). You can still see much of the Passetto by wa

guideSights.name: Palazzo di Giustizia
guideSights.note: Wandering around the shopping and residential district of ''Prati'', close to the Vatican, you may notice rather a lot of lawyers' nameplates outside buildings. This is also Rome's legal district because of the proximity of the ''Palazzo di

guideSights.name: Ponte Sant'Angelo
guideSights.note: This is a footbridge connecting Castel Sant'Angelo with the other side of the Tiber. It is a Roman bridge completed in 134 AD by Hadrian, to give access to his newly constructed mausoleum. Pilgrims used this bridge to reach St Peter's Basil

guideSights.name: Villa Doria Pamphili
guideSights.note: A large villa and 180-ha park that is a major recreation area for Romans, and a popular spot for joggers. One unusual feature of the grounds is the colony of coypus (swamp beavers) around the lake. Natives of South America these ones are de

guideSights.name: Olympic Stadium
guideSights.note: The stadium is on the west bank of River Tiber, about three km directly north of the Vatican. It is part of a sports complex that was built for the 1960 Olympic Games, including the Olympic swimming pool and the tennis complex where the ann

guideSights.name: Santa Passera
guideSights.note: This church can be an interesting deviation if you are passing through its neighbourhood. It is believed to be the grave of the Saints Ciro and Giovanni, killed during the time of the Emperor Diocletian. The original name was ''Abba Cyrus''

guideSights.name: Museum of the Walls
guideSights.note: Porta San Sebastiano is a gate in the amazingly well-preserved Aurelian Walls. Inside and upstairs is a museum dedicated to the construction of the walls and their recent restoration. You can take a walk along the top of the walls. At the m

guideSights.name: Tomb of Priscilla
guideSights.note: A 1st-century tomb surrounded by two farmhouses from the Middle Ages, one of which used to be a cheese store. Rather hidden behind a high wall, the tomb is rarely open to the public. You might be lucky on a Sunday: on the third Sunday of ev

guideSights.name: The Catacombs of San Callisto
guideSights.note: Although started in the 2nd century, San Callisto has had many more recent burials, including 16 popes. The burial arcades are almost 20 km long.

guideSights.name: The Catacombs of San Domitilla
guideSights.note: The Catacombs of Domitilla are considered to be the best preserved of all Roman catacombs. They are the only ones still to contain bones. Domitilla also has a subterranean basilica, much of which was reconstructed in 1870.

guideSights.name: Basilica and catacombs of San Sebastiano
guideSights.note: The first basilica was constructed in the 4th century and dedicated to San Sebastian, a martyr of the 3rd century. Sebastian's remains were transferred to St. Peter's in 826, prior to a Saracen assault when the church was destroyed. The cur

guideSights.name: Fosse Ardeatine
guideSights.note: This was the site of the slaughter in 1944 of 335 Italians, including many Jews from the Ghetto, in retaliation for a Partisan attack on German troops in Rome. The caves where the massacre took place are now a National Monument and Memorial

guideSights.name: Jewish Catacombs
guideSights.note: These are underneath a property known as Vigna Randanini. The catacombs are much smaller than the Christian catacombs and much less easy to visit. Groups are limited to twelve people at any one time and you need to take your own lighting!

guideSights.name: Caffarella Park
guideSights.note: Caffarella Park covers an area of 339 ha and is part of the larger Appia Antica park. It contains both a working farm and numerous Roman ruins, some quite well preserved and is a great place for a stroll or cycle away from Rome’s traffic.

guideSights.name: Circus of Maxentius
guideSights.note: This well-preserved Roman circus was built at the beginning of the fourth century. It was part of an imperial villa built by Maxentius and the complex also contains the Mausoleum of his son, Romolo.

guideSights.name: Tomb of Cecilia Metella
guideSights.note: The mausoleum of Cecilia Metella, who died in 69 BC, is the best preserved monument on the Appian Way and dominates the surroundings. In the Middle Ages it was transformed into a fortress and battlements were added. At that time there was c

guideSights.name: Capo di Bove
guideSights.note: This archaeological site displays the thermal baths of the villa of the wealthy Herod Atticus. Also in the complex is a restored villa, until 2002 a private residence, that has an exterior completely covered with pieces from Roman ruins, in

guideSights.name: Villa dei Quintilii
guideSights.note: This impressive villa covers 23 hectares. It can be accessed from the Via Appia Nuova (Bus 118) or through Via Appia Antica 251. Parts can be seen from the Appian Way at around the 5th mile just after No 251. The villa was built by Maximus

guideSights.name: Casal Rotondo
guideSights.note: Casal Rotondo is the biggest mausoleum on the Appian Way, at about the sixth mile. It now incorporates a small private villa, originally a farmhouse. It is not known for whom it was built. The wall of fragments next to it, constructed by Lu

guideSights.name: Parco degli Acquedotti (Aqueduct Park)
guideSights.note: This pleasant park contains very well-preserved ruins of two aqueducts and some of the original surface of the Roman Via Latina. Gets crowded on Sundays but almost empty the rest of the week during term time. Good place for joggers.

guideSights.name: Abbey of the three fountains (Abazzia delle tre fontane)
guideSights.note: A truly quiet oasis close to the hustle and bustle of EUR. There are three churches in this complex and the doors are open all day, unlike city churches. The monks produce a range of products such as liqueurs, chocolate and honey, as well a

guideSights.name: L. Pigorini National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography
guideSights.note: An ethnographic collection of around 60,000 pieces from European indigenous cultures. Documents evolution from the Palaeolithic age to the Iron Age.

guideSights.name: Museo della Civilta Romana (Museum of Rome's Civilization)
guideSights.note: Perhaps most famous for a large model of imperial Rome, but also has a large display of various aspects of ancient Rome, using plaster casts, models and reconstructions of works found in museums throughout the world.

guideSights.name: Rome's Planetarium
guideSights.note: Regular shows plus an excellent astronomical museum.

guideSights.name: Square Colosseum
guideSights.note: Constructed around the 1940s as the centrepiece of the EUR, but unused for a long time. It was restored before 2015 when the luxury fashion label Fendi moved in.

guideSights.name: San Paolo fuori le Mura
guideSights.note: Also known as St Paul Outside the Walls. This is on the outskirts of Rome in an otherwise drab modern neighborhood. The enormous basilica is a faithful reconstruction, finished in 1854, of the ancient basilica which burned down in 1823. Par

guideSights.name: Santa Passera
guideSights.note: This church can be an interesting deviation if you are passing through its neighbourhood. It is believed to be the grave of the Saints Ciro and Giovanni, killed during the time of the Emperor Diocletian. The original name was ''Abba Cyrus''

guideSights.name: Centrale Montemartini Museum
guideSights.note: This delightful museum provides an interesting juxtaposition between the buildings and equipment of Rome's first electricity generating plant and the exhibits, which are mainly from excavations of Roman sites. A combined ticket with the mus

guideSights.name: Jubilee Church
guideSights.note: A modern church designed by the world-famous architect Richard Meier. Completed in 2003 and built as a project to socially revive the surrounding Tor Tre Teste area.

guideSights.name: Trevi Fountain
guideSights.note: Completed in 1762 to a design by Nicola Salvi, this spectacular Baroque fountain features a mythological sculptural composition of Neptune, god of the sea, flanked by two Tritons: one Triton labours to control a violent sea-horse, the other

guideSights.name: Via Veneto
guideSights.note: It was immortalised in 1960 by the ''Federico Fellini'' film ''La Dolce Vita''. It is also the location of the US Embassy, in the massive Palazzo Margherita. Via Veneto went into a period of decline in the 1980s but has returned to populari

guideSights.name: Servian walls
guideSights.note: Remains of the first city walls, built in the early 4th century BC and attributed to king Servius Tullius.

guideSights.name: Capuchin Monastery
guideSights.note: Built after 1631, the crypt of the church contains a macabre display - a series of chapels decorated with the bones of 3700 dead friars. The bones are glued to the walls and ceilings in bizarre and striking decorations.

guideSights.name: Le Quattro Fontane
guideSights.note: Four fountains from the time of Pope Sixtus V when much of Rome was redeveloped. A reclining deity is the theme of each sculpture. This is a busy intersection and if you don't look twice you may miss these exquisite examples of Roman mythol

guideSights.name: Palazzo Massimo
guideSights.note: A magnificent collection of ancient Roman sculptures, mosaics and wall paintings, including the famous paintings from the Imperial-era villa discovered under the Villa Farnesina, as well as the dining room from the Empress Livia's villa at

guideSights.name: Palazzo Barberini
guideSights.note: This remarkable building, designed partly by Bernini, houses the National Gallery of Ancient Art, and includes some famous paintings by Filippo Lippi and Caravaggio, as well as Raphael's "La Fornarina".

guideSights.name: Piazza Barberini
guideSights.note: With Bernini's famous Triton Fountain. Via Veneto starts here too.

guideSights.name: Palazzo del Quirinale
guideSights.note: Home of the President of the Italian Republic, and the Quirinal Gardens. Built in 1573 as a papal summer residence, and has since also served as the residence for the pope and later for the king of Italy.

guideSights.name: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane
guideSights.note: A very small and beautiful church, the first design commission of Francesco Borromini.

guideSights.name: Santa Maria degli Angeli
guideSights.note: This church was built inside the former baths of Diocletian. Very light and airy inside. Note the unusual art on the outside doors. Around solar noon check out the sun's image on Francesco Bianchini's meridian line inside.

guideSights.name: Santa Maria della Vittoria
guideSights.note: Now invaded by readers of Dan Brown's ''Angels and Demons'', this is an interesting Baroque church containing Bernini's "Ecstasy of St. Teresa". Either side of this chapel are characters in what can best be described as theatre boxes. These

guideSights.name: St Paul's Within the Walls
guideSights.note: More modern than most Roman churches: it was not started until 1873. This is Rome’s Episcopalian church. Some very interesting artwork, particularly the mosaics by Edward Burne-Jones of the Pre-Raphaelite school.

guideSights.name: British Embassy
guideSights.note: At the northern end of Via XX Settembre next to the '''Porta Pia''' designed by Michaelangelo. The previous embassy had been destroyed by a terrorist bomb in 1946 and was eventually replaced by this world-renowned modern design by Sir Basil

guideSights.name: Palazzo Colonna
guideSights.note: One of the most splendid (still private) Baroque grand palaces in Rome.

guideSights.name: The Pantheon
guideSights.note: It was built in 27 BCE, by Augustus' right hand man Marcus Agrippa, and later remodeled by the Emperor Hadrian (AD 125-128). This ancient temple was built as a temple to all the gods of the Roman state but has served as a Christian church s

guideSights.name: Largo di Torre Argentina
guideSights.note: Not, as commonly believed, named after the country but after the city of Strasbourg (''Argentoratum'' in Latin), from which came a courtesan of Pope Alexander VI who lived nearby. Four Roman Republican-era temples, Pompey's theater and a Ro

guideSights.name: Temple of Hadrian
guideSights.note: The temple of the Emperor Hadrian was consecrated in 145 AD by Emperor Antoninus Pius. The remains of the antique temple were incorporated into a new building that served as the Papal Customs House. It was finished around 1690 and today acc

guideSights.name: Sant'Andrea della Valle
guideSights.note: Minor basilica in 17th-century baroque style with good art inside. In a smaller Italian city, this might be a prime attraction, but in Rome, with its abundance of great churches, this is merely a pleasant church of secondary interest to vis

guideSights.name: Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza
guideSights.note: This little church is hard to find but well worth the extra effort although it is often closed when you get there. One of Borromini's masterpieces. It is located only a block from Piazza Navona, but not usually visible from the street, as y

guideSights.name: Santa Maria sopra Minerva
guideSights.note: This church is literally right next to the Pantheon. It is one of Rome's only Gothic churches, and well worth looking inside, although its plain square façade makes it look inconspicuous from outside. Excellent stained glass windows.

guideSights.name: San Luigi dei Francesi
guideSights.note: This church is roughly halfway between Piazza Navona and the Pantheon. It is most notable for a side chapel which contains three Caravaggio masterworks: "The Calling of St. Matthew", "St. Matthew and the Angel" and "Martyrdom of St. Matthew

guideSights.name: Sant'Ignazio
guideSights.note: Between the Pantheon and Via del Corso. A stunning example of Baroque art. The ceiling frescoes are especially fine, including a trompe l'oeil dome by the master Andrea Pozzo.

guideSights.name: Sant'Agnese in Agone
guideSights.note: By Borromini, reputed to be on the spot where St. Agnes was martyred in the 4th century AD. This lovely basilica church is small with an almost circular interior. It is undergoing rehabilitation and the facade and dome are hidden in scaffol

guideSights.name: Santa Maria dell'Anima
guideSights.note: Contains the tomb of Pope Adrian VI, the last non-Italian pope before Pope John Paul II.

guideSights.name: Santa Maria della Pace
guideSights.note: The church was built by order of Pope Sixtus VI (della Rovere). The campanile was erected in 1504 by Bramante and the church has frescoes of the four sibyls by Raphael in its interior.

guideSights.name: Campo de' Fiori
guideSights.note: If it is sunny, you'll catch a few young people and older gentlemen sitting at the base of a statue in the middle of the open space. The statue is a brooding, hooded Giordano Bruno—an excommunicated Dominican monk and one of the earliest co

guideSights.name: Piazza Navona
guideSights.note: The pride of Baroque Rome, was established towards the end of the 15th century, and preserves the shape of the ancient Stadium of Domitian. The buildings surrounding the square stand where the spectators once sat, watching the spectacle of

guideSights.name: Piazza Colonna
guideSights.note: Where the building of the Italian Government, Palazzo Chigi is situated. Also there is a marvelous carved column—hence the name—dating back to Imperial Rome.

guideSights.name: Piazza della Minerva
guideSights.note: A small piazza just behind the Pantheon. The centerpiece is a statue of an elephant by Bernini with an ancient obelisk on its back.

guideSights.name: Piazza di Sant'Ignazio
guideSights.note: Small and attractive piazza tucked away in a neighborhood near Pantheon.

guideSights.name: Piazza di Monte Citorio
guideSights.note: Where you can find the building of the House of Representatives.

guideSights.name: Piazza di Pasquino
guideSights.note: Small piazza about 20 m (65 ft) from Piazza Navona, behind the Brazilian Embassy. There is a statue named "Pasquino", according to a legend named after a tailor who used to work nearby and had a reputation for complaining. The statue has be

guideSights.name: Via Giulia
guideSights.note: An example of urban planning that goes back to Pope Julius II, who, in 1508, envisioned it as a street that would connect all major government buildings. It is around a kilometer long and is in a straight line, an unusual feature for the ti

guideSights.name: Via de Coronari
guideSights.note: In the Middle Ages pilgrims on their way to St. Peter's had to pass through the Via dei Coronari in order to cross the Tiber at Ponte St. Angelo. The street got its name from the people who sold rosaries to the pilgrims. It follows the anci

guideSights.name: The Ghetto
guideSights.note: The Ghetto lies between the island in the River Tiber and the Theatre of Marcellus and includes Rome’s synagogue. It was established in 1555 as a result of a Papal Bull by Pope Paul IV that required all Jews to live in the area, considered

guideSights.name: Palazzo della Cancelleria
guideSights.note: This remarkable building served as the site of the Apostolic Chancellery, or offices of the Pope, for centuries, and now houses a Vatican court. Tucked behind the facade is also the Basilica of San Lorenzo in Damaso, an ancient Roman house

guideSights.name: Palazzo Farnese
guideSights.note: Since 1871 this has been the French Embassy. This 16th-century palace contains an important fresco cycle by Annibale Carracci and houses a library of collections by the French school in Rome, particularly on Roman archaeology. Note the two

guideSights.name: Palazzo della Sapienza
guideSights.note: This building housed the University of Rome from the middle of the 15th century until 1935. The splendid interior courtyard was created by Giacomo della Porta. The inside church of Sant'Ivo (see above) is one of the masterpieces of the arch

guideSights.name: Palazzo Altemps
guideSights.note: Simple and elegant lines make up this building, whose construction began in 1480 for Count Girolamo Riario, nephew of Papa Sisto IV, and was taken up by architect Martino Longhi for the new owner, Cardinal Marco Sittico Altemps. Today it ho

guideSights.name: Palazzo Taverna
guideSights.note: The building is in one of the most hidden corners of the city center among Piazza Navona and Castel Sant'Angelo. It served as residence for the Orsini family. Nowadays it is private property and one can only glance at the courtyard and the

guideSights.name: Palazzo Crivelli
guideSights.note: This building also known as the Doll House was built in the 16th century. It is unique for the quantity and quality of the decorations—lions' heads, satyrs and disfigured heads that adorn the facade attributed to the sculptor Giulio Mazzoni

guideSights.name: Palazzo Spada
guideSights.note: This building was erected in the 16th century for Cardinal Girolamo Capodiferro. One century later it was acquired by another powerful Cardinal, Bernardino Spada, and was restored by Borromini, who created the forced perspective optical ill

guideSights.name: Palazzo Madama
guideSights.note: This palace of the 16th century was erected by the famous Medici family. It was the residence of Cardinals Giovanni and Giuliano Medici, later Pope Leo X. and Clement VII. Catherine de Medici, Pope Clement VII's niece lived here until her m

guideSights.name: Palazzo Massimo alle Colonne
guideSights.note: The palace was built by the architect Baldassare Peruzzi on behalf of the Massimo family. The former palace was destroyed during the pillage of Rome in 1527. The Massimo family can be traced back to Quintus Fabius Maximus who defeated Hanni

guideSights.name: Palazzo del Collegio Romano
guideSights.note: The Collegio Romano was a college of the Jesuit order. Many popes, cardinals and bishops were educated here. Since 1870 it has been a secular (non-monastic) school. The coat of arms on the doorway is that of Pope Gregory XIII (1572–1585). T

guideSights.name: Hosteria dell'Orso
guideSights.note: A historical inn where reputedly the Italian poet Dante Aligheri and French travellers of the 16th century, including the poets François Rabelais and Michel de Montaigne, stayed.

guideSights.name: Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi
guideSights.note: By Bernini, in the very centre of Piazza Navona. Incorporates an Egyptian obelisk and symbolises four of the world's great rivers (the Ganges, the Nile, the Danube and the Plata), representing the four continents known at the time.

guideSights.name: Fontana del Moro
guideSights.note: At the southern end of the Piazza, designed by Bernini but the main statue of the Moor was done by Giacomo della Porta and the other statues are 19th-century copies of the originals.

guideSights.name: Fontana del Nettuno
guideSights.note: A 19th-century addition to the square, made to balance the Fontana del Moro.

guideSights.name: Fontanella del Facchino
guideSights.note: Like Pasquino, the Facchino is one of the so-called "speaking figures" which are peculiar to Rome. He is looking out of the Banco di Roma building. The man depicted is holding a barrel in his hands and is carrying water. It is sometimes sai

guideSights.name: Fontana delle Tartarughe
guideSights.note: A pleasant fountain in an out-of-the-way square. It was originally meant to have four dolphins rather than turtles but the dolphins proved to be too large for the water pressure so the turtles were added as an afterthought.

guideSights.name: Museo Napoleonico
guideSights.note: The museum is dedicated to Napoleon Bonaparte and his family. After Napoleon's death in 1821 the Pope gave permission to his family to settle down in Rome. His sister married Prince Camillo Borghese.

guideSights.name: Obelisco di Montecitorio
guideSights.note: An ancient Egyptian obelisk brought to Rome in 10 BC.

guideSights.name: Santa Maria Minerva Obelisk
guideSights.note: One of Bernini's masterpieces, an obelisk on the back of an elephant.

guideSights.name: Colosseum
guideSights.note: Known properly as the Flavian Amphitheatre, this most famous of Roman landmarks takes its name from the giant statue of the emperor Nero that once stood near this location. The amphitheatre was capable of seating 50,000 spectators for anima

guideSights.name: Palatine Hill
guideSights.note: Contains the ruins of several large villas that belonged to wealthy Roman families. You can buy a combined ticket for the Palatine Hill, the Roman Forum and the Colosseum here, avoiding the long lines at the Colosseum. While the Imperial an

guideSights.name: The Roman Forum
guideSights.note: If stones could talk: these hallowed ruins were the most powerful seat of government in the world. To stand in the political, legal and religious centre of the whole Roman Empire brings shivers down one's spine. It is the best way of imagin

guideSights.name: Temple of Antoninus Pius and Faustina
guideSights.note: Built in 141 AD and dedicated to the Empress Faustina; after her husband emperor Antoninus Pius died in 161 AD the temple was rededicated to the couple.

guideSights.name: Basilica Aemilia
guideSights.note: Completed in 179 BC.

guideSights.name: Temple of Divine Julius Caesar
guideSights.note: Finished in 29 BC, marks the spot of Caesar's spontaneous cremation and Mark Antony's funeral speech, made famous by Shakespeare in his play ''Julius Caesar'' ("Friends, Romans, Countrymen, lend me your ears ...").

guideSights.name: Arch of Titus
guideSights.note: Built in 81 AD by the emperor Domitianus in dedication to his brother Titus, who died earlier that year and reigned as emperor from 79-81, overseeing the opening of the Colosseum in 80 and the eruption of Mt Vesuvius the previous year.

guideSights.name: Tabularium
guideSights.note: The remains of the ancient Roman archives, where Cicero and Seneca did research. Visible from the Forum and accessible through the Capitoline Museum.

guideSights.name: Arch of Constantine
guideSights.note: Located a short walk west of the Colosseum, this well-preserved monumental arch was erected (soon after 315) to commemorate the victory of Constantine, the first Christian emperor, over his rival Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridg

guideSights.name: Piazza del Campidoglio
guideSights.note: On top of the Capitoline hill. The piazza was designed by Michelangelo. The Capitoline Museum is housed in the palaces flanking the piazza. You can walk behind the Palazzo Senatorio, where Rome's government meets, to a wonderful '''viewpoin

guideSights.name: Piazza Venezia
guideSights.note: More of an enormous traffic circle than a piazza, but a good central location. The centerpiece is the enormous Vittorio Emanuele Monument (aka the Wedding Cake or the Typewriter) with the Capitoline hill next door. Mussolini used to harangu

guideSights.name: Vittorio Emanuele Monument
guideSights.note: Built in honour of Victor Emmanuel, the first king of a unified Italy, this vast structure may appear to be solid white marble but actually contains many rooms inside. There are two permanent museums, one on Italian Reunification and one on

guideSights.name: Colle Oppio
guideSights.note: This is the attractive park on the hillside directly west of the Colosseum. Visible ruins in the area come from the '''Baths of Trajan'''. These baths were built on the top of the ruins of '''Domus Aurea''' - the Golden House of Nero (the C

guideSights.name: Trajan's Markets
guideSights.note: On the other side of the Via dei Fori Imperiali to the Roman Forum. Well-preserved market area that doubled as a way of stopping the Quirinal Hill from collapsing. Below in the Forum is Trajan's Column, built in 113 with reliefs depicting t

guideSights.name: Mamertine Prison
guideSights.note: Romans and leaders of Rome's defeated enemies were imprisoned here where they either died of starvation or strangulation. According to legend, St. Peter was also imprisoned here.

guideSights.name: Theatre of Marcellus
guideSights.note: Unusual ancient Roman theatre with apartments built on top.

guideSights.name: San Clemente
guideSights.note: A great little cathedral to visit, lovingly looked after by Irish Dominicans. There is an excavated older church below the medieval church you enter and a Mithraeum (temple to Mithras, whose cult was very popular with Roman soldiers from th

guideSights.name: Santo Stefano Rotondo
guideSights.note: Unusual and fascinating round church dedicated to St. Stephen. It is the national church of Hungary in Rome. Dating from the 5th century this is believed to be the largest round church in the world. Charles Dickens described its wall painti

guideSights.name: San Pietro in Vincoli
guideSights.note: The chains that allegedly held St. Peter are displayed in a case before the altar. More importantly, contains the impressive statue of Moses by Michelangelo. It's close to the Colosseum, but a little hard to find. Take the steps opposite th

guideSights.name: Santa Maria in Aracoeli
guideSights.note: Ballroom-like church which crowns part of the Capitoline Hill. Don't be fooled by the plain stone exterior.

guideSights.name: Chiesa del Gesù
guideSights.note: This is one of the two main Jesuit churches in Rome, the other being the nearby Sant'Ignazio. The interior is Mannerist art on steroids. Simply astounding.

guideSights.name: San Nicola in Carcere
guideSights.note: Church built on the site of three Roman pagan temples, which can be explored underground for a small fee paid at a desk near the church entrance.

guideSights.name: Basilica dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo al Celio
guideSights.note: According to the legendary passio, two brothers, John and Paul, who were officials at the imperial court, suffered martyrdom in 362 in their home on the Caelian hill, during the reign of emperor Flavius Claudius Julianus. This basilica dedi

guideSights.name: Santa Prassede
guideSights.note: Fantastic Byzantine mosaics and some other interesting artwork. Not to be missed. 30 minutes are sufficient for a relaxed visit.

guideSights.name: Santa Pudenziana
guideSights.note: A very ancient church named after a saint who was in 1969 removed from the Roman Catholic calendar of saints for the lack of details of her life. But the church retains the name and is well worth visiting for an excellent 4th-century mosaic

guideSights.name: Musei Capitolini
guideSights.note: The two museums are on opposite sides of the Piazza del Campidoglio, It is recommended to [http://www.ticketclic.it book tickets online]

guideSights.name: Museo Capitolino
guideSights.note: Built in the 17th century to a design based on an architectural sketch by Michelangelo. Highlights include the ancient Colossus of Constantine statue (the Colosseum was probably named for another giant statue, the Colossus of Nero which sto

guideSights.name: Palazzo dei Conservatori
guideSights.note: Also based on a Michelangelo architectural plan, this compact gallery is well endowed in classical sculpture and paintings. Highlights include the small 1st-century-BC bronze ''Lo Spinario'', a Greek statue of a little boy picking a thorn f

guideSights.name: National Museum of the Palazzo di Venezia
guideSights.note: In the very heart of the city center, the building was for centuries ago the seat of the Venice embassy. Today it houses a museum and art galleries.

guideSights.name: Palazzo Doria Pamphilj
guideSights.note: Good collection of Renaissance and Baroque art, including by Velasquez, Titian, Raphael, and Bernini, all owned by the Doria Pamphilj family. Excellent audio guides really bring the paintings to life.

guideSights.name: Ara Pacis
guideSights.note: Ara Pacis is an altar to peace commissioned by the Roman Senate on 4 July 13 BC to honor the triumphal return from Hispania and Gaul of Augustus. It is universally recognised as a masterpiece. Following discovery of this work under a buildi

guideSights.name: Mausoleo di Augusto

guideSights.name: Catacombe di Priscilla
